rationale: Real demand and a C-level custom-rate proxy, but per-rig throughput is an analyst guess and the ~6-week window strands equipment most of the year. Part 137 plus pesticide licensing takes months; FCC Covered List threatens fleet supply; operator count is growing fast and retailers can buy their own drones. Realistic yr3 ~$40-100k.
red_flags: Aerial rate is Indiana manned-aircraft proxy, not drone
Equipment stranding risk from FCC actions

rationale: Low-capital, license-free and paid on delivery, but retailers give sampling away to win fertilizer sales, the fall window is short, and fields repeat only every 2-4 years. Per-acre pricing is assumed. Local seasonal labor business with a small profit pool; independent-data niche with farm managers is real but thin.
red_flags: Profit ceiling ~$5k/mo by record own admission

rationale: Seed is a mandatory annual input, but dealer commissions are missing entirely, appointments are controlled by seed companies favoring farmer-dealers, and sales run on multi-year personal relationships a non-farmer outsider lacks. Extreme township-level competition and no wedge. Low capital does not offset low probability of meaningful profit.

Only farm-count data supports this; dealer margins, territory availability and transaction sizes are all assumed. Hardware margins are thin, demo inventory ties up cash, OEM dealership precision departments dominate, and farm capex is cyclical. In-season service reputation can build a regional book, but an outsider without ag credibility starts far behind.

Genuine safety-driven need and paid-on-completion, but no pricing or frequency data; demand is a short pre-harvest window and many farmers self-perform. Engulfment and dust-explosion liability make insurance a likely margin killer. Local seasonal crew business with a low ceiling; robot-assisted angle is a modest wedge.

5-15% buy-sell margins on inventory plus 6-12 months of grower credit, against co-ops bundling agronomy, credit and rebates. Record itself admits no credible small-scale entry strategy. Launch capital $100-500k breaches the capital gate, hazmat storage and pesticide dealer licensing add burden. Consumable demand is the only positive.

Strongest structure in this group: tiny capital, near-pure-margin residual book on essential spend, transferable and rep-scalable. But commission rates are unverified, the niche is saturated with telemarketing brokers and supplier direct sales, and the ICC ABC license needs an experienced individual plus 90-180 days. Realistic yr3-5 ~$80-200k.

Capacity prices are A-level but the partner revenue share is missing, and the 5-15% share yields only a few thousand dollars per site. CSPs sell direct, set the terms, and the price collar ends after 2027/28; all-hours availability rules deter some curtailers. Good bundle with brokerage, weak as a standalone business.
red_flags: Revenue depends on PJM auction outcomes

rationale: Value arithmetic is sound but only for customers whose contracts pass capacity costs through, a share the record never measures. Peak alerts are routinely given free by brokers, CSPs and suppliers; savings-share fees lag 12+ months; value collapses if capacity prices normalize after the collar. A feature of the brokerage bundle, not a business.

No-cost contingency offer lowers buyer resistance, capital is negligible, and LLM bill extraction genuinely cuts audit labor. But hit rates, refund sizes and look-back limits are unknown, fees lag months, audits are largely one-time, and franchise networks already canvass the space. Realistic yr3 ~$60-150k with reps and monitoring add-ons.
red_flags: Schooley Mitchell scale is self-claimed D

rationale: Utility program implementers already give audits free, federal incentives (179D, 25C) are ending, and incumbent comps show thin 6% operating margins. Real money requires project development with 3-9 month cycles and engineering credibility the founder lacks. Low capital but a weak, incentive-dependent profit pool for a newcomer.
red_flags: Incumbent margins cited as if new-entrant

rationale: Mature, saturating market: LED retrofits are one-time, incentive-dependent and low-bid, with 20-35% gross margins and rebate-assigned receivables lagging. Requires licensed electricians and ICC Part 462 certification. Remaining un-retrofitted stock is unmeasured. Reachable buyers but a shrinking runway and no repeat revenue.
red_flags: Incumbent ESCO margins used as proxy

rationale: Illinois Shines volumes (B) show a growing rural fleet needing recurring O&M and vegetation work, and subcontracting to national O&M firms is a realistic first step. But O&M pricing is missing, buyers are concentrated asset owners with credibility walls, electrical PM needs hired electricians, and federal credit changes may slow new builds.
red_flags: Federal credit termination timing not verified

rationale: Federal 30C and vehicle credits have ended, so install demand is likely softening; maintenance pricing is literally a placeholder. ICC Part 469 certification needs a qualified person and electricians are scarce. Uptime-maintenance niche for networked chargers is plausible but unmeasured, competing with OEM networks and electrical contractors.

Commission rates and transaction value are both missing, so economics are unsupported. 852 designees already compete, program issued 21 warnings and 11 suspensions, and the model relies on door-to-door commission canvassers under heavy consumer-protection scrutiny. Developer contracts are concentrated, revenue is one-time per subscriber and bounded by IPA program capacity.

25D expired, so homeowner demand faces a cliff; PY2025-26 approvals likely include pull-forward. Extreme competition among 974 approved vendors, CAC-heavy door-to-door and digital-lead acquisition, 15-30% gross margins and lagging REC payments. Record itself says no compelling entry strategy. Poor risk-adjusted economics for a newcomer.

Zero sources cited, so economics are pure assumption, but the model is sound from industry knowledge: monthly consumable chemistry plus service, high chemical markup, sticky multi-year accounts, and an established independent-operator segment. Main walls are technical credibility, risk-averse switching and treatment-failure liability. Realistic yr3-5 ~$100-200k with hired technicians.
